report.summary: Reviewed canary.py chunk 2 (lines 281-...): probe builders/checkers, ProbeSpec, PROBES registry. Claims mostly kept; one uncheckable due to cross-module constants.
risks: check_arrival | medium | tail regex uses word boundaries; tail words with non-alphanumeric chars would fail. Need to inspect _TAIL_WORDS.
check_instruction | low | _normalise strips trailing periods; if the model outputs 'OK-nonce.' it is accepted, but the prompt says 'nothing else' — this may be too lenient.
build_anchoring | low | _anchor_pair uses _ANCHOR_SETS and _ORDINALS defined elsewhere; their format is not verified here.
check_anchoring | medium | word extraction uses [a-z]+; words with hyphens or numbers are split, but decoy/correct are presumably simple words.
check_comprehension | medium | _NUMBER_RE matches '1' but also 'one' etc. If reply contains '11' it matches '1' and could be wrong. The regex is not anchored.
ProbeSpec | low | severity validated against SEVERITIES defined elsewhere; not checked here.
PROBES registry | medium | only three of four probes are shown; the comprehension probe is missing from the registry, which is a potential omission.

claims.text: Both incidents were truncation, in OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, so one token cannot catch both
claims.why: The prompt requires both head and tail tokens, and check_arrival requires both, so it catches both directions.

claims.text: Requiring BOTH tokens back is what makes a single cheap probe cover both.
claims.why: check_arrival checks both head and tail presence.

claims.text: It also closes the obvious false pass: a model that lost the tail may still echo the head token while complaining about the cut, and that reply is correctly rejected because it cannot contain a tail word it never received.
claims.why: check_arrival requires both tokens; if tail missing, returns 'tailword_absent' or 'both_absent'.

claims.text: ~40 lines of filler is roughly 800 tokens: long enough that a transport which truncates has something to truncate, and far enough under the Ollama usable input window that the probe itself never provokes the failure it measures.
claims.why: The claim about token counts and Ollama's window depends on external constants and model specifics not in this chunk.

claims.text: Accept only if BOTH ends of the prompt demonstrably arrived.
claims.why: The function checks head_ok and tail_ok and returns True only if both are true.

claims.text: The tail came back but the head did not: the prompt was HEAD-truncated (over-budget Ollama) or the lane never saw the opening bytes.
claims.why: The branch when head_ok is False and tail_ok is True returns 'nonce_absent', matching the comment.

claims.text: Strip TRANSPORT artefacts only -- never content.
claims.why: The function removes code fences, surrounding quotes, whitespace, and trailing period; it does not remove other content.

claims.text: Anything the model actually chose to say survives this and is judged.
claims.why: Only specific patterns are removed; other text remains.

claims.text: It knew the answer and said more anyway. That is the degradation this probe exists for -- a lane that is alive and no longer obedient.
claims.why: The function returns 'not_exact' when the reply contains the wanted string but is not exactly equal.

claims.text: Detect a lane that copied the decoy instead of answering.
claims.why: The function returns 'anchored_on_decoy' if the decoy word is present.

claims.text: Reported as a QUALITY signal by :data:`PROBES`: a model anchoring on a prior turn is alive, reachable and useless for reasoning work.
claims.why: The PROBES registry defines severity 'quality' for anchoring, but the full registry is not fully shown (only three probes). The claim about calling it nothing is not verifiable here.

claims.text: Decoy present WINS over a correct word also being present: a reply containing both is a reply that regurgitated the transcript.
claims.why: The code checks has_decoy first and returns 'anchored_on_decoy' regardless of has_correct.

claims.text: The nonce is deliberately NOT in this prompt: the answer is a digit, and a nonce full of digits would give a lazy checker something to trip over.
claims.why: The prompt does not include the nonce; it asks for a number.

claims.text: Exactly one of them mentions a rollback.
claims.why: _summaries replaces one decoy with a target from _SUMMARY_TARGETS, all of which mention rollback, while decoys do not (as per the constant names).

claims.text: A probe is (prompt, checker) and the checker is deterministic Python.
claims.why: ProbeSpec has build, check, expect callables; the check functions are deterministic given nonce and reply.

observations.what: PROBES registry shows only three probes (arrival, instruction, anchoring); comprehension is defined but not registered in the shown portion.
check_arrival tail regex uses word boundaries; if _TAIL_WORDS contains punctuation, the check may fail.
_normalise strips trailing period; a reply 'OK-nonce.' is accepted as exact, which may be too lenient for 'Nothing else' instruction.
check_comprehension regex matches first number-like token; a reply with '11' would match '1' and could be wrong.
ProbeSpec severity validation uses SEVERITIES which is not defined in this chunk; uncheckable but likely fine.
